title: Water dripping under the car
h1: Why is water dripping under my car?
metaDesc: Water dripping under your car? Find out in a few questions if it's normal A/C condensation or a coolant leak, how urgent it is, and what to do next.
synonyms: is it normal for my car to leak water
intro: Most of the time, clear water dripping under a car is normal condensation from the A/C or the exhaust. But coolant can look a lot like water, and a coolant leak can lead to overheating. A few quick questions will help you narrow down which one you're dealing with and what to do.
safety: If the temperature gauge is in the red or you see steam from under the hood, pull over and turn off the engine.
Never open the radiator or coolant cap while the engine is hot. The coolant is under pressure and can scald you.
Coolant is poisonous to pets and children. Clean up puddles right away.

q_temp.q: Is the temperature gauge higher than normal, or is a temperature or coolant warning light on?
q_temp.help: On most cars the needle normally sits near the middle once the engine is warm. Some cars show a blue or red thermometer light instead of a gauge.

opts.a: Yes, it's high or in the red, or I see steam
No, the gauge is normal and no warning lights
I'm not sure

q_where.q: Where is the water dripping from?

opts.a: Under the middle or front passenger side, roughly below the dashboard
From the tailpipe at the back
Under the very front of the car, near the radiator
Somewhere else, or I'm not sure

q_ac.q: Had you been using the A/C, or the defroster, before it dripped?
q_ac.help: The defroster often runs the A/C compressor automatically to dry the air, even when you haven't pressed the A/C button.

opts.a: Yes, and the water is clear with no smell
Yes, but the liquid is colored, slimy or smells sweet
No, the A/C was off
I'm not sure

q_exhaust.q: What does it look like at the tailpipe?

opts.a: A few drips of clear water, maybe a little white vapor that clears once the engine warms up
Thick white smoke that keeps going after it's warm, or a sweet smell
I'm not sure

q_feel.q: Wipe up a little with a white paper towel. What is it like?
q_feel.help: Coolant is usually green, orange, pink, yellow or blue, feels slightly slimy, and smells sweet. Plain water has no color, smell or slickness.

opts.a: Clear, no smell, feels like plain water
Colored, slightly slimy, or smells sweet
Bright blue and smells like glass cleaner
Oily or slick, and doesn't feel like water
I'm not sure

q_coolant_amount.q: How much coolant does it seem to be losing?
q_coolant_amount.help: With the engine cold, look at the see-through coolant overflow tank. It has MIN and MAX (or LOW and FULL) marks.

opts.a: Just a few drops, and the tank is still between the marks
A steady drip or a puddle, or the tank is below the low mark
It's pouring or spraying, or the tank is empty
I'm not sure

result.title: The engine may be overheating, and the liquid may be coolant
result.now: Pull over safely, turn off the engine and don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you see steam, stay back and don't open the hood until it stops.
If you're still moving and need a few seconds to reach a safe place to stop, turn the heater on full blast. It pulls some heat away from the engine.
If you see smoke rather than steam, or smell fuel or burning, move away from the car.
result.why: A high temperature reading along with dripping liquid often means coolant is escaping. Driving an overheating engine can warp or crack expensive parts within minutes.

causes.name: Leaking radiator or hose
causes.clues: Colored, sweet-smelling liquid under the front of the car.

causes.name: Failed water pump
causes.clues: Drips from the front of the engine, sometimes with a whine or grinding.

causes.name: Cooling fan not working
causes.clues: It overheats mostly when stopped in traffic.

causes.name: Head gasket failure
causes.clues: White, sweet-smelling exhaust and coolant loss with no obvious drip.

you: Once the engine is fully cold, check the coolant overflow tank level.
shop: Combustion gas (block) test for a head gasket leak

result.title: This sounds like normal A/C condensation
result.now: Clear, odorless water here is usually normal and needs no repair. To be sure, check the coolant tank when the engine is cold over the next week and keep an eye on the temperature gauge.
if: If the passenger floor gets wet inside the car, the A/C drain may be blocked. Get it cleared.
If the A/C stops dripping on a hot, humid day but runs cold, the drain may be clogging. Watch for a damp carpet.
If the coolant level drops, the drip turns colored or sweet-smelling, or the temperature gauge rises, have the cooling system checked.
result.why: The A/C pulls moisture out of the cabin air, and it drains out through a small tube under the car, usually near the front passenger footwell. On hot, humid days it can leave a surprisingly big puddle of plain water.

causes.name: Normal A/C condensation
causes.clues: Clear, odorless water under the front passenger area after running the A/C or defroster.
causes.against: If the liquid is colored, slimy or sweet-smelling, it isn't just condensation.

causes.name: Rain or car wash water running off
causes.clues: It's been raining, or the car was recently washed.

you: Touch and smell a drop. It should feel and smell like plain water.
Check that the coolant tank level stays steady over the next week.
shop: A/C drain tube check if the inside floor gets wet

result.title: Water from the tailpipe is usually normal condensation
result.now: This is usually normal. Keep an eye on your coolant level and the temperature gauge for the next few weeks to be sure.
if: If the white smoke doesn't clear after the engine is fully warm, or it smells sweet, have the cooling system checked soon.
If the coolant level keeps dropping with no visible leak, get it checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, or you see steam, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: Burning fuel makes water vapor. On cold starts and short trips it condenses inside the exhaust and drips out the tailpipe. Once the exhaust heats up, it should dry out.

causes.name: Normal exhaust condensation
causes.clues: Cold weather, short trips, and drips that stop once the car is warm.

causes.name: Coolant getting into the engine
causes.clues: Thick white smoke that stays when warm, a sweet smell, and a dropping coolant level.
causes.against: If the coolant level stays steady, this is less likely.

you: Note whether the drips and vapor stop after 10–15 minutes of driving.
Check the coolant tank level when cold, once a week for a few weeks.
shop: Cooling system pressure test if coolant is dropping

result.title: Coolant may be leaking into the engine and burning
result.now: Stop driving it. Once the engine is cold, check the coolant tank level, then have it towed or have a mobile mechanic check it.
if: If the temperature gauge rises at all, shut the engine off right away.
If the engine oil on the dipstick looks milky, like chocolate milk, coolant may be mixing with the oil. Don't start it again.
result.why: Thick, sweet-smelling white smoke that doesn't clear often means coolant is getting into the cylinders and burning. That can point to a head gasket or cracked part, which a shop will confirm with tests before any repair, and driving on it can overheat the engine and cause major damage.

causes.name: Blown head gasket
causes.clues: Steady white smoke, coolant loss with no visible leak, and possible overheating.

causes.name: Cracked cylinder head or block
causes.clues: The engine overheated badly at some point.

causes.name: Leaking intake gasket (some engines)
causes.clues: Coolant loss and a rough idle.

you: Check the coolant level when the engine is cold.
Pull the oil dipstick and look for a milky, light-brown color.

result.title: Clear, odorless water is often condensation or rain runoff
result.now: Check the coolant tank level when the engine is cold. If it's between the marks and stays there over the next few days, this water is most often condensation or runoff.
if: If the coolant level drops over the next week, the drip may be watered-down coolant. Have the cooling system checked.
If water also shows up inside the car, check our guide to water leaking inside the car.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, or you see steam, pull over and turn off the engine.
result.why: Plain water with no color, smell or slickness is usually A/C condensation or rain and wash water dripping off the body. Coolant mixed with a lot of water can look clear, though, so the coolant level is the real test.

causes.name: A/C condensation
causes.clues: It drips under the passenger side after the A/C or defroster has run.

causes.name: Rain or wash water
causes.clues: It rained or the car was washed recently.

causes.name: Diluted coolant
causes.clues: The coolant tank level slowly drops, or the drip is near the radiator.

you: Check the coolant tank level when cold, then again in a few days.
Put cardboard under the car overnight on a dry night.
shop: Cooling system pressure test if the level drops

result.title: It looks like windshield washer fluid
result.now: Check the washer fluid tank and its hoses for cracks or a loose connection. Refill it and see if the level drops.
if: If the washer fluid empties quickly, the tank, pump or a hose may be cracked. Get it fixed so you're not left without washers in bad weather.
If the fluid looks green or orange and smells sweet rather than like glass cleaner, it may be coolant. Check the coolant level.
result.why: Washer fluid is usually bright blue and smells like glass cleaner. Its tank sits near the front of the car, and cracked tanks or loose hoses are common.

causes.name: Cracked washer fluid tank
causes.clues: It drips near a front corner, especially after filling.

causes.name: Loose or split washer hose
causes.clues: It leaks when you use the washers.

causes.name: Leaking washer pump seal
causes.clues: Drips at the bottom of the tank.

you: Fill the washer tank and watch for drips.
Use the washers and look for leaks from the hoses.

result.title: If it's oily, it isn't water. Another fluid is leaking
result.now: Note the color on the paper towel and where it drips, then check your engine oil, brake fluid, transmission and power steering fluid levels. Have the leak identified within a day or two.
if: If the drip is near a wheel, or it's clear to yellowish and slick, it could be brake fluid. Don't drive it until it's been inspected, even if the brake fluid level looks OK.
If the brake fluid level is low or the brake pedal feels soft, don't drive it. Have it towed.
If you can't tell what it is, or it leaves a puddle bigger than a plate overnight, have it inspected before driving much.
If it smells like gasoline, don't start the engine. Keep sparks and flames away and have it towed.
If a warning light comes on or the steering feels heavy, pull over and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Water doesn't feel slick. An oily liquid means engine oil, transmission fluid, power steering fluid or brake fluid. The color and where it drips help narrow it down, and a shop can confirm it.

causes.name: Engine oil
causes.clues: Brown or black, under the engine.

causes.name: Transmission or power steering fluid
causes.clues: Red, pink or amber.

causes.name: Brake fluid
causes.clues: Clear to yellowish and slick, often near a wheel.

you: Check every fluid level you can reach.
Take a photo of the puddle and the paper towel for the shop.

result.title: Check the coolant level to rule out a leak
result.now: When the engine is cold, look at the coolant overflow tank and note where the level sits. Check it again in a few days.
if: If the level drops, have the cooling system checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge ever climbs above normal, pull over and turn off the engine.
If you see steam or smell something sweet, stop the engine and have it checked before driving further.
result.why: Most clear drips turn out to be condensation, but a slow coolant leak can look similar. A dropping coolant level is the simplest way to tell them apart.

causes.name: A/C or exhaust condensation
causes.clues: Clear water, and the coolant level stays steady.

causes.name: Slow coolant leak
causes.clues: A sweet smell, colored drips, or a coolant level that keeps dropping.

you: Check the coolant tank level when cold.
Put cardboard under the car overnight and look at the color of any drips.

result.title: This sounds like a small coolant seep, often from a hose, clamp or the radiator
result.now: Check the coolant level when cold every few days, top it up with the type in your owner's manual if needed, and book a check.
if: If the level keeps dropping or the drips get bigger, get it checked within a few days.
If the temperature gauge rises above normal, pull over and turn off the engine.
If you see steam, white smoke from the exhaust, or smell coolant inside the car, have it checked before driving further.
result.why: A few drops with a steady level means a slow seep. If the level holds steady it can usually wait for a booked check, but cooling system leaks tend to grow, and running low on coolant leads to overheating.

causes.name: Loose clamp or aging hose
causes.clues: Dried, crusty coolant residue on a hose end.

causes.name: Radiator seep
causes.clues: Residue or dampness on the radiator, at the very front.

causes.name: Water pump starting to leak
causes.clues: Drips or residue near the front of the engine, by the belt.

you: Look for crusty white, green or pink residue on hoses and the radiator.
Track the coolant level when cold.
shop: Dye test if the source isn't clear

result.title: An active coolant leak that needs checking soon
result.now: When the engine is cold, top up the coolant to the full mark with the type in your owner's manual. Limit driving to what's necessary, watch the temperature gauge closely, and get it checked within a few days. If you can't top it up, don't drive it.
if: If the temperature gauge rises above normal or you see steam, pull over and turn off the engine. Don't restart it.
If the level drops a lot after one short trip, or you see a stream rather than drips, don't drive it. Have it towed.
result.why: A steady drip or a low tank means the engine is losing coolant faster than is safe. Without enough coolant it will overheat, which can cause serious engine damage.

causes.name: Leaking radiator hose
causes.clues: Drips at a hose end, or a soft, swollen hose.

causes.name: Leaking radiator
causes.clues: Drips from the very front, under the radiator.

causes.name: Water pump leak
causes.clues: Drips from the front of the engine, near the belt.

you: Note how much coolant you add and how quickly the level drops.
Put cardboard under the car overnight to mark the drip spot.

result.title: A major coolant leak. The engine could overheat within minutes
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you see steam, stay back and don't open the hood or the coolant cap until it has fully cooled.
If the temperature gauge was in the red before you stopped, tell the shop. They may want to check for overheating damage.
result.why: With coolant pouring out or the tank empty, the engine has nothing to carry heat away. Running it, even briefly, risks warping or cracking engine parts.

causes.name: Burst or split radiator hose
causes.clues: A sudden gush, often with steam.

causes.name: Cracked radiator or overflow tank
causes.clues: Coolant pouring from the front of the car.

causes.name: Failed water pump
causes.clues: Coolant streaming from the front of the engine.

shop: Hose, radiator and water pump inspection
